In June 2011, a new attraction called Cliffwalk was added to the park.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-5)

## Incidents

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Capilano_Suspension_Bridge&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Incidents")]

In September 1999, a woman dropped her 18-month-old child with [Down syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down_syndrome "Down syndrome") off the bridge. She claimed she stumbled accidentally and the child slipped from her grasp. The child was not seriously injured.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-:0-7) The woman lost legal custody of her child to the child's father as a result of the incident.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-8) The woman took legal action against the owner of the bridge, her ex-husband and the [Federal Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Justice_(Canada) "Department of Justice (Canada)").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-9) The case against the owner of the bridge was settled in 2004.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-:0-7)

In 2006, a 300-year-old, 46-tonne Douglas fir tree toppled during a heavy snowstorm,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-10) falling across the western end of the bridge. Park officials closed the bridge temporarily while repairs were performed.

On June 6, 2010, a teenage tourist on a class trip from California climbed over a railing and fell more than 30 metres (98 ft) from a fenced-off viewing platform near the bridge. By the time rescue workers came to his aid, the victim was dead.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-11) The official [RCMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Canadian_Mounted_Police "Royal Canadian Mounted Police") finding was that the teen was under the influence of [LSD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lysergic_acid_diethylamide "Lysergic acid diethylamide") at the time of the incident.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-12)

On June 2, 2012, a 30-year-old tourist from [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario") died after falling near the bridge. Police say the victim was hiking through trails near the popular attraction when he climbed over a railing and fell to the riverbed below.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-13)

## Popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Capilano_Suspension_Bridge&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Popular culture")]

The bridge has been featured as a setting in episodes of several television series, including _[MacGyver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacGyver\_(1985\_TV\_series) "MacGyver (1985 TV series)")_, _[Sliders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sliders\_(TV\_series) "Sliders (TV series)")_, _[The Crow: Stairway to Heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Crow:\_Stairway\_to\_Heaven "The Crow: Stairway to Heaven")_, and _[Psych](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psych "Psych")_.

In 1974, social psychologists Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron conducted a well-known experiment on the bridge. Men approached by a female researcher on the bridge were more likely to call her later than men approached on a more solid bridge across the river. Dutton and Aron argued that this supported the theory that the men were [mis-attributing the arousal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misattribution_of_arousal "Misattribution of arousal") caused by fear to sexual attraction toward the woman.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-14) This research supported [Stanley Schachter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Schachter "Stanley Schachter")'s [two-factor theory of emotion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-factor_theory_of_emotion "Two-factor theory of emotion").

In June 2019, [Korean Pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-pop "K-pop") group [NCT 127](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCT_127 "NCT 127") created a video of their visit to the Capilano Suspension Bridge as part of the social media documenting their world tour _NCT 127: The Origin_.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-15)

The bridge has appeared in the racing games _[Mario Kart Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario\_Kart\_Tour "Mario Kart Tour")_ and _[Mario Kart 8 Deluxe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario\_Kart\_8 "Mario Kart 8")_ as a part of the first lap in the "Vancouver Velocity" race track.

The **Capilano Suspension Bridge** is a [simple suspension bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_suspension_bridge "Simple suspension bridge") crossing the [Capilano River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_River "Capilano River") in Upper [Capilano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_(North_Vancouver) "Capilano (North Vancouver)"), British Columbia, Canada, in the [District of North Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(district_municipality) "North Vancouver (district municipality)").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-2) The current bridge is 140 metres (460 ft)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-structurae-1) long and 70 metres (230 ft) above the river. It is part of a private facility with an admission fee and draws over 1.2 million visitors per year.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Capilano_Suspension_Bridge&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

The bridge was originally built in 1889[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-3) by George Grant Mackay, a Scottish civil engineer and park commissioner for [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver"). It was originally made of hemp ropes with a deck of cedar planks and was replaced with a wire cable bridge in 1903. In 1910 [Edward Mahon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Mahon "Edward Mahon") purchased the Capilano Suspension Bridge. "Mac" MacEachran purchased the Bridge from Mahon in 1935 and invited local natives to place their [totem poles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Totem_pole "Totem pole") in the park, adding a native theme. In 1945, he sold the bridge to Henri Aubeneau.

The bridge was completely rebuilt in 1956.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-asce-4)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a7/Tourists_on_the_Treetop_Walk.jpg/250px-Tourists_on_the_Treetop_Walk.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tourists_on_the_Treetop_Walk.jpg)

Treetops Adventure

The park was sold to Nancy Stibbard, the current owner, in 1983. Annual attendance increased, and in May 2004, Treetops Adventures was opened, consisting of seven footbridges suspended between old-growth Douglas fir trees on the west side of the canyon, forming a walkway up to 30 metres (98 ft) above the forest floor.

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge%2C_Vancouver%2C_Canada_%28July_2016%29_2.jpg/250px-Capilano_Suspension_Bridge%2C_Vancouver%2C_Canada_%28July_2016%29_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Capilano_Suspension_Bridge,_Vancouver,_Canada_(July_2016)_2.jpg)

Capilano Suspension Bridge

In June 2011, a new attraction called Cliffwalk was added to the park.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-5)

## Incidents

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Capilano_Suspension_Bridge&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Incidents")]

In September 1999, a woman dropped her 18-month-old child with [Down syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down_syndrome "Down syndrome") off the bridge. She claimed she stumbled accidentally and the child slipped from her grasp. The child was not seriously injured.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-:0-7) The woman lost legal custody of her child to the child's father as a result of the incident.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-8) The woman took legal action against the owner of the bridge, her ex-husband and the [Federal Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Justice_(Canada) "Department of Justice (Canada)").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-9) The case against the owner of the bridge was settled in 2004.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-:0-7)

In 2006, a 300-year-old, 46-tonne Douglas fir tree toppled during a heavy snowstorm,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-10) falling across the western end of the bridge. Park officials closed the bridge temporarily while repairs were performed.

On June 6, 2010, a teenage tourist on a class trip from California climbed over a railing and fell more than 30 metres (98 ft) from a fenced-off viewing platform near the bridge. By the time rescue workers came to his aid, the victim was dead.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-11) The official [RCMP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Canadian_Mounted_Police "Royal Canadian Mounted Police") finding was that the teen was under the influence of [LSD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lysergic_acid_diethylamide "Lysergic acid diethylamide") at the time of the incident.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-12)

On June 2, 2012, a 30-year-old tourist from [Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ontario "Ontario") died after falling near the bridge. Police say the victim was hiking through trails near the popular attraction when he climbed over a railing and fell to the riverbed below.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-13)

## Popular culture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Capilano_Suspension_Bridge&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Popular culture")]

The bridge has been featured as a setting in episodes of several television series, including _[MacGyver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MacGyver\_(1985\_TV\_series) "MacGyver (1985 TV series)")_, _[Sliders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sliders\_(TV\_series) "Sliders (TV series)")_, _[The Crow: Stairway to Heaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Crow:\_Stairway\_to\_Heaven "The Crow: Stairway to Heaven")_, and _[Psych](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psych "Psych")_.

In 1974, social psychologists Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron conducted a well-known experiment on the bridge. Men approached by a female researcher on the bridge were more likely to call her later than men approached on a more solid bridge across the river. Dutton and Aron argued that this supported the theory that the men were [mis-attributing the arousal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Misattribution_of_arousal "Misattribution of arousal") caused by fear to sexual attraction toward the woman.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-14) This research supported [Stanley Schachter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_Schachter "Stanley Schachter")'s [two-factor theory of emotion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Two-factor_theory_of_emotion "Two-factor theory of emotion").

In June 2019, [Korean Pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K-pop "K-pop") group [NCT 127](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCT_127 "NCT 127") created a video of their visit to the Capilano Suspension Bridge as part of the social media documenting their world tour _NCT 127: The Origin_.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_Suspension_Bridge_Park#cite_note-15)

The bridge has appeared in the racing games _[Mario Kart Tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario\_Kart\_Tour "Mario Kart Tour")_ and _[Mario Kart 8 Deluxe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mario\_Kart\_8 "Mario Kart 8")_ as a part of the first lap in the "Vancouver Velocity" race track.

The **District of North Vancouver**, commonly **North Vancouver** or **North Van**, is a [district municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_municipality "District municipality") in [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia"), Canada, situated north of the city of [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver") across the [Burrard Inlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burrard_Inlet "Burrard Inlet"). It surrounds the respective [City of North Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(city) "North Vancouver (city)") on three sides, and the remaining fellow [North Shore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Shore_(Greater_Vancouver) "North Shore (Greater Vancouver)")[municipality of West Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Vancouver "West Vancouver") on the other, and is part of the [Metro Vancouver Regional District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Vancouver_Regional_District "Metro Vancouver Regional District").

It is largely characterized as a relatively quiet, affluent suburban hub home to many middle and upper-middle-class families. Homes in the District of North Vancouver generally range from mid-sized family bungalows to very large luxury houses. A number of dense multi-family and mixed-use developments have popped up across the district in recent years; however, the district remains a primarily suburban municipality. It is served by the [Royal Canadian Mounted Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Canadian_Mounted_Police "Royal Canadian Mounted Police"), [British Columbia Ambulance Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia_Ambulance_Service "British Columbia Ambulance Service"), and the District of North Vancouver Fire Department.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

First, the Spanish arrived, giving their name to Vancouver's Spanish Banks, and, in 1792, Captain [George Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Vancouver "George Vancouver") explored the local shores.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)#cite_note-5) But it was not until 1862 that the first attempt was made to harvest the North Shore's rich stands of timber, leading to fuller settlement of the area that would later become North Vancouver.

The first industry on the North Shore was Pioneer Mills, founded in 1862 to log the huge trees of the coastal rainforest. After twice changing hands, the operation was bought by [Sewell ("Sue") Prescott Moody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sewell_Moody "Sewell Moody") in 1865. Near where the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool grain elevators now stand, the town of Moodyville grew up and stood as the main centre of activity on the North Shore until the mill closed in 1901. The first school was established in Moodyville. The second, Central School, opened in 1902 in a building that still stands as part of what is now [Presentation House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presentation_House?action=edit&redlink=1 "Presentation House (page does not exist)") at 3rd Street and Chesterfield Avenue, the current home of the North Vancouver Museum and Archives.

In 1891, the first municipality on the North Shore was formed as the District of North Vancouver. It stretched across the North Shore from [Horseshoe Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horseshoe_Bay,_West_Vancouver,_British_Columbia "Horseshoe Bay, West Vancouver, British Columbia") to [Deep Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Cove,_North_Vancouver "Deep Cove, North Vancouver") but omitted Moodyville. In the early years of the 20th century, a real estate boom took place, with speculators – including the British poet [Rudyard Kipling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudyard_Kipling "Rudyard Kipling") – eager to turn a quick dollar. A new community began to take shape. In 1902, the Hotel North Vancouver was built; in 1905, the first bank, a branch of the [Bank of North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_North_America "Bank of North America"), opened. A newspaper, the Express, commenced publication in 1905, and in 1906 the [British Columbia Electric Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia_Electric_Railway "British Columbia Electric Railway") began streetcar service.

Industry, particularly shipbuilding, became central, with the nearby stands of trees a rich resource for a society in which ships, houses, and most other manmade things were constructed mainly of wood. The Wallace Shipyards moved in 1906 to the area just east of Lonsdale Avenue, drawn by the arrival of electricity. Over the years, this company, later known as [Burrard Dry Dock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burrard_Dry_Dock "Burrard Dry Dock") and then [Versatile Pacific Shipyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Versatile_Pacific_Shipyards?action=edit&redlink=1 "Versatile Pacific Shipyards (page does not exist)"), became a major force in the local economy. Many of the shipyard's buildings still stand although the company has now ceased operations.

Economic prosperity and rapid growth in the Lower Lonsdale area of North Vancouver led to the establishment in 1907 of the separate [City of North Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(city) "North Vancouver (city)"), with a population of approximately 1,500. [West Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Vancouver "West Vancouver") separated from the district in 1912. Apart from the addition of [Moodyville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moodyville,_British_Columbia "Moodyville, British Columbia") in 1915, the boundaries of the city have not changed, even though far more people now call the district home.

Communications with Vancouver have always been an important factor in the development of the North Shore. The first ferry service was supplied by "Navvy Jack’s" rowboat in 1866. In 1867, the Sea Foam established a regular ferry service that continued until 1958. The [SeaBus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SeaBus "SeaBus") re-established water transportation in 1977. Rail service was slower in developing. While the [Pacific Great Eastern Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Great_Eastern_Railway "Pacific Great Eastern Railway") inaugurated a 12.7-mile run from North Vancouver to [Whytecliff Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whytecliff_Park "Whytecliff Park") in 1914, it was not until the completion of the first [Second Narrows Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Narrows_Bridge "Second Narrows Bridge") in 1925 that rail and road links with the [Lower Mainland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Mainland "Lower Mainland") supplemented the local ferry service.

Early plans for North Vancouver were ambitious. However, early grandiose plans met with a number of setbacks. The real estate boom was overtaken by a worldwide depression in 1913 and then [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") delayed many projects. The depression that began in 1929, coupled with disruptions to communications over the Second Narrows caused by ships colliding with the bridge, led to economic difficulties and severe tax shortfalls. Both the city and the district were placed in receivership in 1933. But the opening of the second road crossing, the [Lions Gate Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lions_Gate_Bridge "Lions Gate Bridge"), in 1938 was a significant factor in making the North Shore more accessible. And the war years led to an economic revival of North Vancouver, especially because of the many ships built in the [Burrard Dry Dock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burrard_Dry_Dock "Burrard Dry Dock") at the foot of Lonsdale for the Canadian war effort.

In the postwar years, the city and the District of North Vancouver boomed, with most of the growth taking place in the district because of its greater land resources.

Since 2018, there have been proposals to amalgamate the District of North Vancouver with the City of North Vancouver into a single North Vancouver.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)#cite_note-7) Surveys have shown that the majority of the municipalities' residents support the idea, and many do not even know that the city and the district are separate entities.

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/CapilanoRiverRegPark-river.jpg/250px-CapilanoRiverRegPark-river.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CapilanoRiverRegPark-river.jpg)

The [Capilano River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_River "Capilano River").

The District of North Vancouver is separated from [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver") by the [Burrard Inlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burrard_Inlet "Burrard Inlet"). It can be accessed by the [Lions' Gate Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lions'_Gate_Bridge "Lions' Gate Bridge"), the [Ironworkers Memorial Second Narrows Crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ironworkers_Memorial_Second_Narrows_Crossing "Ironworkers Memorial Second Narrows Crossing"), and the [SeaBus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SeaBus "SeaBus") passenger ferry.

The district is bounded by the [Capilano River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_River "Capilano River") to the west, [Indian Arm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Arm "Indian Arm") to the east, [Burrard Inlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burrard_Inlet "Burrard Inlet") to the south, and the [Coast Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coast_Mountains "Coast Mountains") to the north. It sprawls in an east–west direction across the mountain slopes and is characterized by rugged terrain and steep and winding roadways. While there is no true urban core within the district, there are a number of separate commercial neighbourhood centres. These include (from west to east): [Edgemont Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgemont_Village "Edgemont Village"), [Upper Lonsdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Lonsdale "Upper Lonsdale"), [Lynn Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynn_Valley "Lynn Valley"), Main Street, Parkgate, and [Deep Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Cove,_North_Vancouver "Deep Cove, North Vancouver").

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/CapilanoLake.jpg/250px-CapilanoLake.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CapilanoLake.jpg)

Capilano Lake.

The district has much in common with [West Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Vancouver "West Vancouver") and the City of North Vancouver. Together, these three municipalities are commonly referred to as the [North Shore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Shore_(Greater_Vancouver) "North Shore (Greater Vancouver)"). Most of the residents of the district live in single-family dwellings. Except for a few more historical areas, much of the development of the district has occurred since the 1950s. The City of North Vancouver has considerably higher commercial and residential density.

## Industry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Industry")]

While industry was the engine that propelled North Vancouver for much of the twentieth century, this has now largely been replaced by enterprises more in tune with present economic realities. Many North Shore companies are in the business of creating and marketing high technology.

The television and film industry has made the area the centre of Hollywood North. Filming of the television series _[The X-Files](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_X-Files "The X-Files")_ took place in North Vancouver for five seasons, with many of its "wilderness" sequences shot in the [Lower Seymour Conservation Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Seymour_Conservation_Reserve "Lower Seymour Conservation Reserve") (LSCR).

*   The Capilano Suspension Bridge in a private park carries hikers across the Capilano River to nature trails and a unique rainforest canopy walk (there is an admission fee).
*   The [Lynn Canyon Suspension Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynn_Canyon_Suspension_Bridge "Lynn Canyon Suspension Bridge") is in a District of North Vancouver public park (free admission). Also at the park is the Lynn Canyon Ecology Centre.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)#cite_note-10)
*   [Grouse Mountain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grouse_Mountain "Grouse Mountain") is a ski hill and a tourist destination reached by either a [gondola lift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gondola_lift "Gondola lift") or the famous Grouse Grind hike.
*   [Mount Seymour Provincial Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Seymour_Provincial_Park "Mount Seymour Provincial Park") is a ski and hiking destination in the district.
*   The [Cleveland Dam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cleveland_Dam "Cleveland Dam") in the [Capilano River Regional Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_River_Regional_Park "Capilano River Regional Park") offers nature trails as well as a fish [hatchery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hatchery "Hatchery"), the Capilano River Hatchery.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)#cite_note-11)
*   [Mount Fromme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Fromme "Mount Fromme") is a mountain bicycling destination.
*   Northlands Golf Course is a public golf course owned and operated by the District of North Vancouver.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)#cite_note-12)
*   [Maplewood Flats Conservation Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maplewood_Flats_Conservation_Area "Maplewood Flats Conservation Area") is a conservation area known for its bird watching and easy to access trails
*   Maplewood Farm is an educational children's farm operated by the District of North Vancouver
*   The [Museum of North Vancouver Archives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_and_Archives_of_North_Vancouver "Museum and Archives of North Vancouver") is part of MONOVA and holds historical records of the North Shore

## Transportation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Transportation")]

The main (and only) highway through the District of North Vancouver is the [Trans-Canada Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Canada_Highway "Trans-Canada Highway") ([Highway 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia_Highway_1 "British Columbia Highway 1")). This crosses over the [Ironworkers Memorial Second Narrows Crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ironworkers_Memorial_Second_Narrows_Crossing "Ironworkers Memorial Second Narrows Crossing") from Vancouver and goes through the district to the western border with West Vancouver.

Public transit is provided by [TransLink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TransLink_(British_Columbia) "TransLink (British Columbia)") and is mostly operated by its subsidiary [Coast Mountain Bus Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coast_Mountain_Bus_Company "Coast Mountain Bus Company"), which runs a network of bus routes throughout the North Shore municipalities, including the [R2 Marine Dr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R2_Marine_Dr "R2 Marine Dr"), as well as buses connecting the municipality with the rest of the Metro Vancouver. The [SeaBus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SeaBus "SeaBus") ferry, which is part of the TransLink system, is also an integral part of the district; it stops at [Lonsdale Quay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonsdale_Quay "Lonsdale Quay"), which connects the North Shore with Vancouver, and [Waterfront station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterfront_station_(Vancouver) "Waterfront station (Vancouver)"), which connects to the [SkyTrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SkyTrain_(Vancouver) "SkyTrain (Vancouver)") network. [West Vancouver Blue Bus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Vancouver_Blue_Bus "West Vancouver Blue Bus") also runs a few routes in the two North Vancouvers, along with the 255, which connects them to West Vancouver. There currently is no [rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_transit "Rapid transit") system in North Vancouver, but TransLink aims to build a [bus rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit") line from Metrotown in Burnaby to Park Royal in West Vancouver as a measure to bring rapid transit to the traffic-congested North Shore.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)#cite_note-13)

## Demographics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Demographics")]

At the [2021 Canadian census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Canadian_census "2021 Canadian census") conducted by [Statistics Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_Canada "Statistics Canada"), North Vancouver had a population of 88,168 living in 32,700 of its 34,179 total private dwellings, a change of 2.9% from its 2016 population of 85,649. With a land area of 160.66 km 2 (62.03 sq mi), it had a population density of 548.8/km 2 (1,421.3/sq mi) in 2021.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)#cite_note-2021census-3)

### Religion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Religion")]

According to the [2021 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Canadian_census "2021 Canadian census"), religious groups in North Vancouver included:[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)#cite_note-2021censusB-14)

*   [Irreligion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreligion_in_Canada "Irreligion in Canada") (48,275 persons or 55.2%)
*   [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity_in_Canada "Christianity in Canada") (29,845 persons or 34.2%)
*   [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_Canada "Islam in Canada") (5,570 persons or 6.4%)
*   [Judaism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaism_in_Canada "Judaism in Canada") (845 persons or 1.0%)
*   [Buddhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism_in_Canada "Buddhism in Canada") (775 persons or 0.9%)
*   [Sikhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikhism_in_Canada "Sikhism in Canada") (550 persons or 0.6%)
*   [Hinduism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinduism_in_Canada "Hinduism in Canada") (295 persons or 0.3%)
*   [Indigenous spirituality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mythologies_of_the_indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Mythologies of the indigenous peoples of the Americas") (15 persons or <0.1%)

In terms of Christianity, 12.4% of the population was Catholic, 11.4% were Protestant, 7.2% were Christian n.o.s, 0.9% were Christian Orthodox, and 2.2% belonged to other Christian denominations and Christian-related traditions.

The **District of North Vancouver**, commonly **North Vancouver** or **North Van**, is a [district municipality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_municipality "District municipality") in [British Columbia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia "British Columbia"), Canada, situated north of the city of [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver") across the [Burrard Inlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burrard_Inlet "Burrard Inlet"). It surrounds the respective [City of North Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(city) "North Vancouver (city)") on three sides, and the remaining fellow [North Shore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Shore_(Greater_Vancouver) "North Shore (Greater Vancouver)")[municipality of West Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Vancouver "West Vancouver") on the other, and is part of the [Metro Vancouver Regional District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Vancouver_Regional_District "Metro Vancouver Regional District").

It is largely characterized as a relatively quiet, affluent suburban hub home to many middle and upper-middle-class families. Homes in the District of North Vancouver generally range from mid-sized family bungalows to very large luxury houses. A number of dense multi-family and mixed-use developments have popped up across the district in recent years; however, the district remains a primarily suburban municipality. It is served by the [Royal Canadian Mounted Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Canadian_Mounted_Police "Royal Canadian Mounted Police"), [British Columbia Ambulance Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia_Ambulance_Service "British Columbia Ambulance Service"), and the District of North Vancouver Fire Department.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

First, the Spanish arrived, giving their name to Vancouver's Spanish Banks, and, in 1792, Captain [George Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Vancouver "George Vancouver") explored the local shores.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)#cite_note-5) But it was not until 1862 that the first attempt was made to harvest the North Shore's rich stands of timber, leading to fuller settlement of the area that would later become North Vancouver.

The first industry on the North Shore was Pioneer Mills, founded in 1862 to log the huge trees of the coastal rainforest. After twice changing hands, the operation was bought by [Sewell ("Sue") Prescott Moody](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sewell_Moody "Sewell Moody") in 1865. Near where the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool grain elevators now stand, the town of Moodyville grew up and stood as the main centre of activity on the North Shore until the mill closed in 1901. The first school was established in Moodyville. The second, Central School, opened in 1902 in a building that still stands as part of what is now [Presentation House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presentation_House?action=edit&redlink=1 "Presentation House (page does not exist)") at 3rd Street and Chesterfield Avenue, the current home of the North Vancouver Museum and Archives.

In 1891, the first municipality on the North Shore was formed as the District of North Vancouver. It stretched across the North Shore from [Horseshoe Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horseshoe_Bay,_West_Vancouver,_British_Columbia "Horseshoe Bay, West Vancouver, British Columbia") to [Deep Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Cove,_North_Vancouver "Deep Cove, North Vancouver") but omitted Moodyville. In the early years of the 20th century, a real estate boom took place, with speculators – including the British poet [Rudyard Kipling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudyard_Kipling "Rudyard Kipling") – eager to turn a quick dollar. A new community began to take shape. In 1902, the Hotel North Vancouver was built; in 1905, the first bank, a branch of the [Bank of North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bank_of_North_America "Bank of North America"), opened. A newspaper, the Express, commenced publication in 1905, and in 1906 the [British Columbia Electric Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia_Electric_Railway "British Columbia Electric Railway") began streetcar service.

Industry, particularly shipbuilding, became central, with the nearby stands of trees a rich resource for a society in which ships, houses, and most other manmade things were constructed mainly of wood. The Wallace Shipyards moved in 1906 to the area just east of Lonsdale Avenue, drawn by the arrival of electricity. Over the years, this company, later known as [Burrard Dry Dock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burrard_Dry_Dock "Burrard Dry Dock") and then [Versatile Pacific Shipyards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Versatile_Pacific_Shipyards?action=edit&redlink=1 "Versatile Pacific Shipyards (page does not exist)"), became a major force in the local economy. Many of the shipyard's buildings still stand although the company has now ceased operations.

Economic prosperity and rapid growth in the Lower Lonsdale area of North Vancouver led to the establishment in 1907 of the separate [City of North Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(city) "North Vancouver (city)"), with a population of approximately 1,500. [West Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Vancouver "West Vancouver") separated from the district in 1912. Apart from the addition of [Moodyville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moodyville,_British_Columbia "Moodyville, British Columbia") in 1915, the boundaries of the city have not changed, even though far more people now call the district home.

Communications with Vancouver have always been an important factor in the development of the North Shore. The first ferry service was supplied by "Navvy Jack’s" rowboat in 1866. In 1867, the Sea Foam established a regular ferry service that continued until 1958. The [SeaBus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SeaBus "SeaBus") re-established water transportation in 1977. Rail service was slower in developing. While the [Pacific Great Eastern Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Great_Eastern_Railway "Pacific Great Eastern Railway") inaugurated a 12.7-mile run from North Vancouver to [Whytecliff Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whytecliff_Park "Whytecliff Park") in 1914, it was not until the completion of the first [Second Narrows Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Narrows_Bridge "Second Narrows Bridge") in 1925 that rail and road links with the [Lower Mainland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Mainland "Lower Mainland") supplemented the local ferry service.

Early plans for North Vancouver were ambitious. However, early grandiose plans met with a number of setbacks. The real estate boom was overtaken by a worldwide depression in 1913 and then [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") delayed many projects. The depression that began in 1929, coupled with disruptions to communications over the Second Narrows caused by ships colliding with the bridge, led to economic difficulties and severe tax shortfalls. Both the city and the district were placed in receivership in 1933. But the opening of the second road crossing, the [Lions Gate Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lions_Gate_Bridge "Lions Gate Bridge"), in 1938 was a significant factor in making the North Shore more accessible. And the war years led to an economic revival of North Vancouver, especially because of the many ships built in the [Burrard Dry Dock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burrard_Dry_Dock "Burrard Dry Dock") at the foot of Lonsdale for the Canadian war effort.

In the postwar years, the city and the District of North Vancouver boomed, with most of the growth taking place in the district because of its greater land resources.

Since 2018, there have been proposals to amalgamate the District of North Vancouver with the City of North Vancouver into a single North Vancouver.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)#cite_note-7) Surveys have shown that the majority of the municipalities' residents support the idea, and many do not even know that the city and the district are separate entities.

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/CapilanoRiverRegPark-river.jpg/250px-CapilanoRiverRegPark-river.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CapilanoRiverRegPark-river.jpg)

The [Capilano River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_River "Capilano River").

The District of North Vancouver is separated from [Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vancouver "Vancouver") by the [Burrard Inlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burrard_Inlet "Burrard Inlet"). It can be accessed by the [Lions' Gate Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lions'_Gate_Bridge "Lions' Gate Bridge"), the [Ironworkers Memorial Second Narrows Crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ironworkers_Memorial_Second_Narrows_Crossing "Ironworkers Memorial Second Narrows Crossing"), and the [SeaBus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SeaBus "SeaBus") passenger ferry.

The district is bounded by the [Capilano River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capilano_River "Capilano River") to the west, [Indian Arm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Arm "Indian Arm") to the east, [Burrard Inlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burrard_Inlet "Burrard Inlet") to the south, and the [Coast Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coast_Mountains "Coast Mountains") to the north. It sprawls in an east–west direction across the mountain slopes and is characterized by rugged terrain and steep and winding roadways. While there is no true urban core within the district, there are a number of separate commercial neighbourhood centres. These include (from west to east): [Edgemont Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgemont_Village "Edgemont Village"), [Upper Lonsdale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_Lonsdale "Upper Lonsdale"), [Lynn Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lynn_Valley "Lynn Valley"), Main Street, Parkgate, and [Deep Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deep_Cove,_North_Vancouver "Deep Cove, North Vancouver").

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fc/CapilanoLake.jpg/250px-CapilanoLake.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:CapilanoLake.jpg)

Capilano Lake.

The district has much in common with [West Vancouver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Vancouver "West Vancouver") and the City of North Vancouver. Together, these three municipalities are commonly referred to as the [North Shore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Shore_(Greater_Vancouver) "North Shore (Greater Vancouver)"). Most of the residents of the district live in single-family dwellings. Except for a few more historical areas, much of the development of the district has occurred since the 1950s. The City of North Vancouver has considerably higher commercial and residential density.

## Industry

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Industry")]

While industry was the engine that propelled North Vancouver for much of the twentieth century, this has now largely been replaced by enterprises more in tune with present economic realities. Many North Shore companies are in the business of creating and marketing high technology.

The television and film industry has made the area the centre of Hollywood North. Filming of the television series _[The X-Files](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_X-Files "The X-Files")_ took place in North Vancouver for five seasons, with many of its "wilderness" sequences shot in the [Lower Seymour Conservation Reserve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Seymour_Conservation_Reserve "Lower Seymour Conservation Reserve") (LSCR).

## Transportation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Transportation")]

The main (and only) highway through the District of North Vancouver is the [Trans-Canada Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Canada_Highway "Trans-Canada Highway") ([Highway 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Columbia_Highway_1 "British Columbia Highway 1")). This crosses over the [Ironworkers Memorial Second Narrows Crossing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ironworkers_Memorial_Second_Narrows_Crossing "Ironworkers Memorial Second Narrows Crossing") from Vancouver and goes through the district to the western border with West Vancouver.

Public transit is provided by [TransLink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TransLink_(British_Columbia) "TransLink (British Columbia)") and is mostly operated by its subsidiary [Coast Mountain Bus Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coast_Mountain_Bus_Company "Coast Mountain Bus Company"), which runs a network of bus routes throughout the North Shore municipalities, including the [R2 Marine Dr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R2_Marine_Dr "R2 Marine Dr"), as well as buses connecting the municipality with the rest of the Metro Vancouver. The [SeaBus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SeaBus "SeaBus") ferry, which is part of the TransLink system, is also an integral part of the district; it stops at [Lonsdale Quay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lonsdale_Quay "Lonsdale Quay"), which connects the North Shore with Vancouver, and [Waterfront station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waterfront_station_(Vancouver) "Waterfront station (Vancouver)"), which connects to the [SkyTrain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SkyTrain_(Vancouver) "SkyTrain (Vancouver)") network. [West Vancouver Blue Bus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Vancouver_Blue_Bus "West Vancouver Blue Bus") also runs a few routes in the two North Vancouvers, along with the 255, which connects them to West Vancouver. There currently is no [rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_transit "Rapid transit") system in North Vancouver, but TransLink aims to build a [bus rapid transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_rapid_transit "Bus rapid transit") line from Metrotown in Burnaby to Park Royal in West Vancouver as a measure to bring rapid transit to the traffic-congested North Shore.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)#cite_note-13)

## Demographics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Demographics")]

At the [2021 Canadian census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Canadian_census "2021 Canadian census") conducted by [Statistics Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statistics_Canada "Statistics Canada"), North Vancouver had a population of 88,168 living in 32,700 of its 34,179 total private dwellings, a change of 2.9% from its 2016 population of 85,649. With a land area of 160.66 km 2 (62.03 sq mi), it had a population density of 548.8/km 2 (1,421.3/sq mi) in 2021.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)#cite_note-2021census-3)

### Religion

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Religion")]

According to the [2021 census](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Canadian_census "2021 Canadian census"), religious groups in North Vancouver included:[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vancouver_(district_municipality)#cite_note-2021censusB-14)

*   [Irreligion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irreligion_in_Canada "Irreligion in Canada") (48,275 persons or 55.2%)
*   [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity_in_Canada "Christianity in Canada") (29,845 persons or 34.2%)
*   [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_Canada "Islam in Canada") (5,570 persons or 6.4%)
*   [Judaism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judaism_in_Canada "Judaism in Canada") (845 persons or 1.0%)
*   [Buddhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism_in_Canada "Buddhism in Canada") (775 persons or 0.9%)
*   [Sikhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikhism_in_Canada "Sikhism in Canada") (550 persons or 0.6%)
*   [Hinduism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinduism_in_Canada "Hinduism in Canada") (295 persons or 0.3%)
*   [Indigenous spirituality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mythologies_of_the_indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas "Mythologies of the indigenous peoples of the Americas") (15 persons or <0.1%)

In terms of Christianity, 12.4% of the population was Catholic, 11.4% were Protestant, 7.2% were Christian n.o.s, 0.9% were Christian Orthodox, and 2.2% belonged to other Christian denominations and Christian-related traditions.

Overview

New Orleans Museum of Art (NOMA), the city’s oldest fine arts institution, opened in 1911 with only nine works of art. Today, the museum hosts an impressive permanent collection of nearly 50,000 artworks. The collection, noted for its extraordinary strengths in French and American art, photography, glass, and African and Japanese works, continues to expand and grow, making NOMA one of the top art museums in the South.

Our Guidelines

##### 1. Make Accessibility Info Easy to Find - Dedicated Website Accessibility Page

Clearly post detailed accessibility information online, covering parking, entrances, interior pathways, site plans, and more.

##### 2. Go Beyond ADA Compliance

Consider walkers, canes, crutches — not just wheelchairs. Provide specifics for a variety of mobility needs. Include people who use different devices in the conversation.

##### 3. Go Beyond ADA Compliance

ADA is the minimum. Strive for real-world accessibility through thoughtful design and ongoing improvements.

##### 4. Visibility = Accessibility

If disabled visitors aren't present, barriers may exist. Transparency and preparation are the keys to inclusion. Empower everyone to attend.

Overview

New Orleans Museum of Art (NOMA), the city’s oldest fine arts institution, opened in 1911 with only nine works of art. Today, the museum hosts an impressive permanent collection of nearly 50,000 artworks. The collection, noted for its extraordinary strengths in French and American art, photography, glass, and African and Japanese works, continues to expand and grow, making NOMA one of the top art museums in the South.

##### 1. Make Accessibility Info Easy to Find - Dedicated Website Accessibility Page

Clearly post detailed accessibility information online, covering parking, entrances, interior pathways, site plans, and more.

##### 2. Go Beyond ADA Compliance

Consider walkers, canes, crutches — not just wheelchairs. Provide specifics for a variety of mobility needs. Include people who use different devices in the conversation.

##### 3. Go Beyond ADA Compliance

ADA is the minimum. Strive for real-world accessibility through thoughtful design and ongoing improvements.

##### 4. Visibility = Accessibility

If disabled visitors aren't present, barriers may exist. Transparency and preparation are the keys to inclusion. Empower everyone to attend.

Overview

New Orleans Museum of Art (NOMA), the city’s oldest fine arts institution, opened in 1911 with only nine works of art. Today, the museum hosts an impressive permanent collection of nearly 50,000 artworks. The collection, noted for its extraordinary strengths in French and American art, photography, glass, and African and Japanese works, continues to expand and grow, making NOMA one of the top art museums in the South.

Our Guidelines

##### 1. Make Accessibility Info Easy to Find - Dedicated Website Accessibility Page

Clearly post detailed accessibility information online, covering parking, entrances, interior pathways, site plans, and more.

##### 2. Go Beyond ADA Compliance

Consider walkers, canes, crutches — not just wheelchairs. Provide specifics for a variety of mobility needs. Include people who use different devices in the conversation.

##### 3. Go Beyond ADA Compliance

ADA is the minimum. Strive for real-world accessibility through thoughtful design and ongoing improvements.

##### 4. Visibility = Accessibility

If disabled visitors aren't present, barriers may exist. Transparency and preparation are the keys to inclusion. Empower everyone to attend.

Overview

New Orleans Museum of Art (NOMA), the city’s oldest fine arts institution, opened in 1911 with only nine works of art. Today, the museum hosts an impressive permanent collection of nearly 50,000 artworks. The collection, noted for its extraordinary strengths in French and American art, photography, glass, and African and Japanese works, continues to expand and grow, making NOMA one of the top art museums in the South.

Our Guidelines

##### 1. Make Accessibility Info Easy to Find - Dedicated Website Accessibility Page

Clearly post detailed accessibility information online, covering parking, entrances, interior pathways, site plans, and more.

##### 2. Go Beyond ADA Compliance

Consider walkers, canes, crutches — not just wheelchairs. Provide specifics for a variety of mobility needs. Include people who use different devices in the conversation.

##### 3. Go Beyond ADA Compliance

ADA is the minimum. Strive for real-world accessibility through thoughtful design and ongoing improvements.

##### 4. Visibility = Accessibility

If disabled visitors aren't present, barriers may exist. Transparency and preparation are the keys to inclusion. Empower everyone to attend.

# New Orleans Museum of Art (NOMA), New Orleans

Serving as the grand entrance to City Park since its establishment in 1911, this fine-arts museum exudes the elegance of classic Greek architecture. With the addition of modern wings, NOMA blends old-world charm with contemporary spaciousness, featuring nearly fifty galleries that house a remarkable permanent collection, including nearly 40,000 objects spanning various historical periods.  
  
 The permanent collection features an array of American and European art, with a strong emphasis on French works, including pieces by renowned artists such as Monet, Renoir, Rodin, Matisse, Picasso, Cornell, and Pollock. Notably, NOMA also showcases the talents of Louisiana artists and offers a diverse selection of art forms, including photography, ceramics, and glassworks from cultures worldwide. The museum takes pride in its significant holdings of African, pre-Columbian, and Asian art.  
  
 In addition to its permanent collection, NOMA hosts a year-round schedule of traveling exhibitions, special events, guided tours, and public programs.   
  
 Tip:  
 Visitors should not miss the Sydney and Walda Besthoff Sculpture Garden, a beautifully landscaped 5-acre area situated behind the main building. This gated garden showcases fifty modern sculptures nestled among lush foliage, lagoons, walking trails, and picturesque bridges. The museum complex also features amenities such as a gift shop, a small theater for film screenings, and the newly renovated Café NOMA by Ralph Brennan, offering a delectable array of artisanal flatbreads, sandwiches, salads, veggie bowls, freshly baked breads, and sweets.

# New Orleans Museum of Art (NOMA), New Orleans

Serving as the grand entrance to City Park since its establishment in 1911, this fine-arts museum exudes the elegance of classic Greek architecture. With the addition of modern wings, NOMA blends old-world charm with contemporary spaciousness, featuring nearly fifty galleries that house a remarkable permanent collection, including nearly 40,000 objects spanning various historical periods.  
  
 The permanent collection features an array of American and European art, with a strong emphasis on French works, including pieces by renowned artists such as Monet, Renoir, Rodin, Matisse, Picasso, Cornell, and Pollock. Notably, NOMA also showcases the talents of Louisiana artists and offers a diverse selection of art forms, including photography, ceramics, and glassworks from cultures worldwide. The museum takes pride in its significant holdings of African, pre-Columbian, and Asian art.  
  
 In addition to its permanent collection, NOMA hosts a year-round schedule of traveling exhibitions, special events, guided tours, and public programs.   
  
 Tip:  
 Visitors should not miss the Sydney and Walda Besthoff Sculpture Garden, a beautifully landscaped 5-acre area situated behind the main building. This gated garden showcases fifty modern sculptures nestled among lush foliage, lagoons, walking trails, and picturesque bridges. The museum complex also features amenities such as a gift shop, a small theater for film screenings, and the newly renovated Café NOMA by Ralph Brennan, offering a delectable array of artisanal flatbreads, sandwiches, salads, veggie bowls, freshly baked breads, and sweets.

# Where I write

### A photographic excursion

Mar 29, 2025

8

3

Share

[![Image 3: An overhead shot of the Louisiana Children's Museum in New Orleans City Park (photo credit: Methun)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FQ4K!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8f189499-3431-4187-ae76-668eee300409_1920x1080.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FQ4K!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8f189499-3431-4187-ae76-668eee300409_1920x1080.jpeg)

_An overhead shot of the Louisiana Children's Museum in New Orleans City Park (photo credit: Methun)_

I have found 2025 to be one wild, rough ride, and I’m sure it’s been the same for many of you. While I’ve really enjoyed writing these weekly newsletters, I know that _Graphic Dead Man Walking_ is not necessarily the most lighthearted reading to grace your inbox each week. So I thought I’d give all of us a break from the usual, somber fare and share with you something very special: the place where I do much of my writing.

I live about 10 minutes’ drive from New Orleans’ City Park. The park’s 1300 acres contain the New Orleans Museum of Art, the Botanical Gardens, a golf course, City Bark dog park, an equestrian center, lakes, bayous, forests, bike trails, an amusement park, children’s Storyland, various sports centers, and much more.

#### Acorn Cafe at the Louisiana Children’s Museum

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!gfjp!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcdc8f493-94c5-46db-89ce-f2b6f712afeb_2364x1330.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!gfjp!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcdc8f493-94c5-46db-89ce-f2b6f712afeb_2364x1330.jpeg)

My favorite parts of the park, nestled behind the Museum of Art, are the Sydney and Walda Besthoff Sculpture Garden on Bayou Metairie, and the Louisiana Children’s Museum, on Little Lake.

At the back of the Children’s Museum is Acorn Cafe, the place I plonk myself a couple of times a week to write. I get there early in the morning when it’s mostly empty. I’ll sit outside whenever the weather’s decent and the pollen is not too thick—in March and April in New Orleans we are beset by the “golden rain of death,” when the beautiful live oaks shed mind-boggling masses of pollen.

As you can see from the photo, I have dressed up my humble iPad with a fancy keyboard. It’s my [Qwerkywriter](https://www.qwerkywriter.com/), which felt like a supreme indulgence when I bought it, but which has proved to be so delightful to type on that I have come to regard it as an essential writing tool.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rvsU!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbb6338ac-6890-4b4d-9971-c8c61b3e81c8_2364x1330.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rvsU!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbb6338ac-6890-4b4d-9971-c8c61b3e81c8_2364x1330.jpeg)

_A closer look at the Qwerkywriter. It has a beautiful, clacky typewriter action and, with the touch of a button, can switch between controlling a tablet, a phone, and a laptop. The carriage return lever works, too, either as a regular carriage return or as a programmable macro._

#### Park wildlife

One of the delights of sitting outside at Acorn is the wildlife. Little Lake is home to brown pelicans, double-crested cormorants, great blue herons and their little blue cousins, great and little egrets, white ibis, and many other birds.

If you peer over the parapet surrounding Acorn and the Children’s Museum, you’ll usually see large numbers of turtles—I’m not sure whether they’re pond sliders, river cooters, or one of several other local species. If you want to make the turtles happy, you can buy a little cup of turtle food from Acorn for a quarter.

If you’re lucky, you might also see Alli, the alligator who seems to like hanging out with the turtles. They clamber over her back and swim and dive around her as they race, at top turtle speed, to get food that’s been tossed to them.

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OwRe!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F02f80acd-6fd8-42c0-83eb-596aa671a3e7_2000x1124.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OwRe!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F02f80acd-6fd8-42c0-83eb-596aa671a3e7_2000x1124.jpeg)

_A brown pelican - Louisiana’s state bird_

#### The Besthoff Sculpture Garden

[![Image 9](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!V6eo!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fda6c387f-f5e7-4405-bc73-d3c398f94ee7_2016x1134.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!V6eo!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fda6c387f-f5e7-4405-bc73-d3c398f94ee7_2016x1134.jpeg)

_Crocodylus - Wangechi Mutu_

Adjoining the Children’s Museum is the Sydney and Walda Besthoff Sculpture Garden. If you ever come to New Orleans, it should be on your must-see list. You can catch a streetcar from downtown right to the gates of City Park, and it’s a five-minute walk to the sculpture garden from there.

If it’s not too hot, I usually walk through the sculpture garden after a writing session. The garden covers almost 12 acres and features around 100 works dotted around a bayou and tucked in among the live oaks, azaleas, iris, and agapanthus. I particularly love the incredibly powerful works by Kenyan-American, Wangechi Mutu.

# Where I write

### A photographic excursion

[![Image 3: An overhead shot of the Louisiana Children's Museum in New Orleans City Park (photo credit: Methun)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FQ4K!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8f189499-3431-4187-ae76-668eee300409_1920x1080.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!FQ4K!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8f189499-3431-4187-ae76-668eee300409_1920x1080.jpeg)

_An overhead shot of the Louisiana Children's Museum in New Orleans City Park (photo credit: Methun)_

I have found 2025 to be one wild, rough ride, and I’m sure it’s been the same for many of you. While I’ve really enjoyed writing these weekly newsletters, I know that _Graphic Dead Man Walking_ is not necessarily the most lighthearted reading to grace your inbox each week. So I thought I’d give all of us a break from the usual, somber fare and share with you something very special: the place where I do much of my writing.

I live about 10 minutes’ drive from New Orleans’ City Park. The park’s 1300 acres contain the New Orleans Museum of Art, the Botanical Gardens, a golf course, City Bark dog park, an equestrian center, lakes, bayous, forests, bike trails, an amusement park, children’s Storyland, various sports centers, and much more.

#### Acorn Cafe at the Louisiana Children’s Museum

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!gfjp!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcdc8f493-94c5-46db-89ce-f2b6f712afeb_2364x1330.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!gfjp!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fcdc8f493-94c5-46db-89ce-f2b6f712afeb_2364x1330.jpeg)

My favorite parts of the park, nestled behind the Museum of Art, are the Sydney and Walda Besthoff Sculpture Garden on Bayou Metairie, and the Louisiana Children’s Museum, on Little Lake.

At the back of the Children’s Museum is Acorn Cafe, the place I plonk myself a couple of times a week to write. I get there early in the morning when it’s mostly empty. I’ll sit outside whenever the weather’s decent and the pollen is not too thick—in March and April in New Orleans we are beset by the “golden rain of death,” when the beautiful live oaks shed mind-boggling masses of pollen.

As you can see from the photo, I have dressed up my humble iPad with a fancy keyboard. It’s my [Qwerkywriter](https://www.qwerkywriter.com/), which felt like a supreme indulgence when I bought it, but which has proved to be so delightful to type on that I have come to regard it as an essential writing tool.

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rvsU!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbb6338ac-6890-4b4d-9971-c8c61b3e81c8_2364x1330.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!rvsU!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fbb6338ac-6890-4b4d-9971-c8c61b3e81c8_2364x1330.jpeg)

_A closer look at the Qwerkywriter. It has a beautiful, clacky typewriter action and, with the touch of a button, can switch between controlling a tablet, a phone, and a laptop. The carriage return lever works, too, either as a regular carriage return or as a programmable macro._

#### Park wildlife

One of the delights of sitting outside at Acorn is the wildlife. Little Lake is home to brown pelicans, double-crested cormorants, great blue herons and their little blue cousins, great and little egrets, white ibis, and many other birds.

If you peer over the parapet surrounding Acorn and the Children’s Museum, you’ll usually see large numbers of turtles—I’m not sure whether they’re pond sliders, river cooters, or one of several other local species. If you want to make the turtles happy, you can buy a little cup of turtle food from Acorn for a quarter.

If you’re lucky, you might also see Alli, the alligator who seems to like hanging out with the turtles. They clamber over her back and swim and dive around her as they race, at top turtle speed, to get food that’s been tossed to them.

Adjoining the Children’s Museum is the Sydney and Walda Besthoff Sculpture Garden. If you ever come to New Orleans, it should be on your must-see list. You can catch a streetcar from downtown right to the gates of City Park, and it’s a five-minute walk to the sculpture garden from there.

If it’s not too hot, I usually walk through the sculpture garden after a writing session. The garden covers almost 12 acres and features around 100 works dotted around a bayou and tucked in among the live oaks, azaleas, iris, and agapanthus. I particularly love the incredibly powerful works by Kenyan-American, Wangechi Mutu.

Overview

New Orleans Museum of Art (NOMA), the city’s oldest fine arts institution, opened in 1911 with only nine works of art. Today, the museum hosts an impressive permanent collection of nearly 50,000 artworks. The collection, noted for its extraordinary strengths in French and American art, photography, glass, and African and Japanese works, continues to expand and grow, making NOMA one of the top art museums in the South.

Our Guidelines

##### 1. Make Accessibility Info Easy to Find - Dedicated Website Accessibility Page

Clearly post detailed accessibility information online, covering parking, entrances, interior pathways, site plans, and more.

##### 2. Go Beyond ADA Compliance

Consider walkers, canes, crutches — not just wheelchairs. Provide specifics for a variety of mobility needs. Include people who use different devices in the conversation.

##### 3. Go Beyond ADA Compliance

ADA is the minimum. Strive for real-world accessibility through thoughtful design and ongoing improvements.

##### 4. Visibility = Accessibility

If disabled visitors aren't present, barriers may exist. Transparency and preparation are the keys to inclusion. Empower everyone to attend.

Overview

New Orleans Museum of Art (NOMA), the city’s oldest fine arts institution, opened in 1911 with only nine works of art. Today, the museum hosts an impressive permanent collection of nearly 50,000 artworks. The collection, noted for its extraordinary strengths in French and American art, photography, glass, and African and Japanese works, continues to expand and grow, making NOMA one of the top art museums in the South.

Our Guidelines

##### 1. Make Accessibility Info Easy to Find - Dedicated Website Accessibility Page

Clearly post detailed accessibility information online, covering parking, entrances, interior pathways, site plans, and more.

##### 2. Go Beyond ADA Compliance

Consider walkers, canes, crutches — not just wheelchairs. Provide specifics for a variety of mobility needs. Include people who use different devices in the conversation.

##### 3. Go Beyond ADA Compliance

ADA is the minimum. Strive for real-world accessibility through thoughtful design and ongoing improvements.

##### 4. Visibility = Accessibility

If disabled visitors aren't present, barriers may exist. Transparency and preparation are the keys to inclusion. Empower everyone to attend.
